extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, journalism students, and media scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for deciding which events become news: substantive, product, and competitive considerations used by reporters, producers, and editors to judge story suitability. Covers source selection, generalist vs. specialist roles, and the fourfold importance test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: All journalists must resort to data limitation so as not to be flooded by more information than they can process quickly and fit into limited air time or print space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers encourage reporters not to shoot unnecessary footage and editors ask reporters to keep files short. General reporters, lacking advance knowledge and a repertoire of angles, face an urgent need to limit data to avoid collapse under too much or conflicting information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managed observation / visibility bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Being new to the scene, general reporters can be managed so that they observe only what sources want them to observe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Television reporters are most easily managed because of highly visible camera crews (example: gruesome acts by troops not performed when cameras are present). As transient visitors, reporters often witness dramatic incidents rather than routine social processes, producing a highlights-oriented view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensitivity to dramatic incidents (seeing highlights)
rubrics_metrics.description: General reporters are most sensitive to the unexpected deviations from what they know or consider to be an accepted value, or to behavior which is abnormal or unusually dramatic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters seek out memorable clashes with taken-for-granted assumptions; this tendency leads them to emphasize highlights and to miss recurring, routine behavior that specialists or sociologists would note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview question shaping and freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: General reporters, freed from restraints of continuing relationships, can more easily ask leading, loaded, or provocative questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such questions may expose sources and produce dramatic television spots or magazine quotes. Beat reporters, who must maintain rapport, tend to remain more polite and restrained (example: White House correspondents avoid overly searching questions lest they be accused of disrespect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inaccuracy risk from transience
rubrics_metrics.description: General reporters' brief contact with unfamiliar sources helps explain the many inaccuracies—some major, most minor—that creep into the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of prior knowledge makes getting names, titles, biographical details, and distinguishing self-serving claims difficult. Reporters may report opinions or guesses as facts; corrections rarely receive as much attention as the original inaccuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic and audience reasons for generalists
rubrics_metrics.description: News is still gathered mostly by generalists because general reporters earn less and are more productive and because they are audience-related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beat reporters produce fewer stories per time period; generalists can be reassigned across beats. Editors and producers—often generalists themselves—prefer generalists because specialists may be 'too technical' for audiences and are less likely to be promoted to management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source availability and suitability (authoritativeness & productivity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources gain access to journalists by being able to supply information and by satisfying considerations of authoritativeness and productivity; this creates repeated contact with a limited set of source types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some sources become institutionalized with news organizations (beat relationships). Powerful, eager sources that can always supply information become frequent news suppliers; exceptions occur during breaking stories or when powerless sources supply dramatic news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on public officials, especially the president
rubrics_metrics.description: The public official is the most frequent and regular source; the president (and White House spokespeople) is especially central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public officials provided 78% of stories in one analysis. The president is seen as 'speaking for the country,' is economical to cover, centralizes information, creates photo opportunities, and is highly productive—thus often the source of the biggest stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Story suitability categories
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine story suitability, journalists employ three categories of considerations: substantive considerations (judge story content and newsworthiness), product considerations (evaluate the 'goodness' of stories), and competitive considerations (test stories for their ability to serve in rivalry among news organizations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many suitability considerations are exclusionary to cope with oversupply of potential news; they are relational and can vary depending on news-supply conditions (e.g., 'slow news day').

rubrics_metrics.name: "Important" versus "Interesting"
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantively, stories can be either 'important' or 'interesting'—the ideal being an important story that is also interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These terms are operational only when linked to subjects and objects (to whom they are important/interesting and by what criteria). Story summaries are condensed for selectors to remain aware of content when applying these qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance: Rank in governmental and other hierarchies
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories become important by rank in governmental and other hierarchies; higher-ranking actors' activities are more important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The governmental hierarchy is a visible, efficient exclusionary device (president most important). Nongovernmental leaders attain importance mainly through contact or conflict with government, their organization's visibility, or prestige. On slow news days, lower-ranked officials can become newsworthy by proposing new policies or dramatic statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance: Impact on the nation and the national interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Importance is assigned to stories that affect the nation, its interests, and its well-being; for foreign news, American involvement or constitutional rights considerations make events important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists often use American foreign-policy frames and national values (ethnocentrism, altruistic democracy, etc.) as quick criteria. Institutions 'not functioning normally' and violations of national values are considered especially newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance: Impact on large numbers of people
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that affect large numbers of people are judged more important; the larger the number affected, the greater the importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalists often make impressionistic judgments about scope using perceptions of population, the potential number affected (e.g., disasters), or assumed similarity of interests across audience segments. Journalistic belief that citizens 'should' be informed can also justify reporting on issues not directly felt by many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance: Significance for the past and future
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories are important if they have significance for the past (anniversaries) or future (potential long-term effects); record-breaking events and 'firsts' are automatically newsworthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predicting future significance is risky and often avoided; journalists prefer easily applied indicators (firsts/records) to avoid being later accused of ignoring historically significant events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusionary versus inclusionary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Many suitability considerations are exclusionary (used to limit the mass of available news) while some are inclusionary (nationalizing local institutions or symbolic complexes to create national relevance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusionary criteria help cope with oversupply; inclusionary moves allow small localities to generate nationally important stories when they symbolize broader themes (example: a county dropping out of welfare programs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of abnormality (protest, violence, and conflict)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abnormality—especially protest and violence—is an easily applied indicator of newsworthiness; high-ranking actors engaging in abnormal behavior are always important news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When protest is plentiful it may be downplayed; when scarce it regains importance. Violent protest or conflict tends to elevate stories; the rank of the target and actors modifies importance. Examples: medical malpractice gained national attention only after protests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation of importance in back-of-the-book sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Back-of-the-book sections try to use front-of-the-book importance considerations where possible, but adapt differently in fields like science, medicine, religion, and arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal and education sections align with federal/governmental importance; other sections balance professional-leader judgments vs. impact on large numbers and historical significance. Critics' judgments can define importance in arts coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product and competitive considerations affecting story emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Product considerations evaluate story 'goodness' (e.g., visuals, interviews); competitive considerations test whether a story serves rivalry (e.g., exclusives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These considerations can affect emphasis and priority rather than pure inclusion/exclusion. A story with exciting film or an exclusive interview may be given higher importance; organizational factors (anchor advocacy, executive preferences) also influence placement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variability and subjectivity in importance judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Importance judgments are made by individuals or small groups and will inevitably differ; competition, organizational culture, and personal interests influence these judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: editors' personal enthusiasms (e.g., Walter Cronkite and space coverage), competitive impulses (seeking excitement), and memory of past successful periods (e.g., Watergate) shape choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead and cover selection rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Television leads and magazine cover stories are chosen mainly from stories that meet one of the four importance considerations; when none do, producers choose running stories or those that touch large numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Back-of-the-book subjects rarely become television leads. Covers serve feedback, commercial, competitive purposes, and are seen as conferring national recognition; exclusives or strong visuals can push a story to lead/covers.
